name: Heart and circulation
function: Pumps blood and oxygen around the body.
measureInSpace: Baseera's station measures heart rate; blood pressure is typed in. NASA records heart rate and blood pressure around flight and requires programs to record, monitor and trend vital signs.
whyCheck: One reading is a snapshot. NASA requires crew health results to be kept so trends can be studied, and Baseera compares you with your own normal.
hazardEffects: After time in microgravity, standing up can make blood pressure and blood flow to the brain hard to keep up, causing light-headedness or fainting. NASA says this is a major concern when crews return to gravity.

whenToAct.crew: Act when the app shows Call surgeon, or if you feel faint, dizzy or have chest pain. Chest pain or fainting: press 'I feel unwell now'.
whenToAct.surgeon: The flight surgeon makes the medical decisions, and the crew medical officer (a crew member trained for the job) helps on board. NASA treats medical decision-making as the crew surgeon's job.

prevention: Drink enough water
Rest, then re-measure before worrying about one reading
NASA's countermeasures for fainting on return include extra fluid and salt before landing, exercise and compression garments

name: Lungs and oxygen
function: Bring in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
measureInSpace: Baseera's station measures blood oxygen (SpO2). Spacecraft also monitor cabin air and alert the crew when oxygen, carbon dioxide or pressure leave safe limits.
whyCheck: Low oxygen can be hard to notice yourself: NASA says its symptoms can be mistaken for fatigue, and thinking can be affected.
hazardEffects: Too little oxygen can cause tiredness, nausea, headache, dizziness, mood changes, poorer sleep and loss of colour, night and side vision. Too much oxygen can slow breathing and heart rate, and raises fire risk.

whenToAct.crew: Act when SpO2 stays low or you feel tired, dizzy, sick or have a headache: check the cabin air alarms and put on an oxygen mask. NASA trains crew to do this at any sign of low oxygen.
whenToAct.surgeon: If the air is the cause, the treatment is supplemental oxygen to fix the shortage.

prevention: Know where the cabin air readings and alarms are
Rest and warm your hands before measuring SpO2
Put on an oxygen mask at any sign of low oxygen

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 003: Habitable Atmosphere, pp. 3, 5-7

name: Brain: mood and sleep
measureInSpace: Mood (1 to 5) and sleep hours are typed in. NASA collects a sleep and team questionnaire monthly and records sleep continuously with a wrist sensor, and tests thinking monthly.
whyCheck: Too little sleep causes fatigue and mistakes, and can lead to low mood and anxiety. NASA notes crew rarely get the full 7 to 9 hours: they average about 6.
hazardEffects: Isolated, confined and extreme environments affect mood and performance. Sleep, workload, low oxygen, food and carbon dioxide all contribute. NASA also lists radiation as a risk to thinking, movement and behaviour.

whenToAct.crew: Act when sleep is short for several days, you feel low or anxious, or you cannot concentrate. Ask for a private psychological conference.
whenToAct.surgeon: NASA schedules routine private medical and psychological conferences, and sleep and fatigue consultations are available as needed.

prevention: Keep your sleep space cool, dark and quiet
Avoid bright and blue light for 1 to 2 hours before bed
Stay in contact with family and keep a routine
Journaling and photographing Earth help manage stress

name: Metabolism and nutrition
function: Turns food and water into energy.
measureInSpace: Blood sugar, water and meals are typed in. NASA assesses nutrition before and after a mission, and notes that on-orbit dietary assessments can help.
whyCheck: Too little food has led to weight loss, bone and muscle loss, weaker immune function and heart deconditioning. Too little water reduces concentration and physical performance.
hazardEffects: In space, food acceptability, space sickness and missed meal times have reduced how much crews eat. ISS crews have drunk about 2 to 2.3 litres a day.

whenToAct.crew: Act when you skip meals, drink little, or your blood sugar is outside the range: eat and drink first, then tell the flight surgeon if it continues.
whenToAct.surgeon: NASA aims for each crew member to get 100% of their calculated energy and nutrient needs, and supplements vitamin D.

prevention: Eat your planned meals
Drink water through the day
Control space sickness: it is essential for a healthy appetite

name: Skin and temperature
function: Protects the body and helps control temperature.
measureInSpace: Baseera's station measures forehead skin temperature, which is not core body temperature. NASA also photographs skin as required before, during and after flight.
whyCheck: A raised temperature can be an early sign of infection. Forehead readings are affected by the room and by exercise, so your own trend matters.
hazardEffects: The cabin environment (temperature, humidity and air) shapes comfort and health, and the spacecraft alerts the crew when it goes outside safe limits.

whenToAct.crew: Act when temperature is at fever level (38 °C or more) or you also feel unwell. A rash that does not fade under a glass needs emergency help.
whenToAct.surgeon: Tell the flight surgeon about skin changes: photographs help the doctors.

prevention: Rest in a comfortable room before measuring
Report new rashes early

name: Bones and muscles
function: Hold the body up and let it move.
measureInSpace: Exercise minutes are typed in. Bone density is NOT measured in flight: NASA checks it before and after flight.
whyCheck: Bone loss is not usually noticed until a problem occurs, so prevention matters. NASA requires countermeasures to keep hip and spine bone density at or above 95% of the pre-mission value.
hazardEffects: Microgravity reduces the load on bones and muscles, which lowers bone density and may raise the risk of fracture. Longer missions, including lunar and Mars, increase the exposure.

whenToAct.crew: Act when you miss exercise sessions, or ask the exercise specialists to adjust your programme.
whenToAct.surgeon: NASA monitors calcium, vitamin D and bone markers throughout an astronaut's life, and the flight surgeon decides on any supplements.

prevention: Do your exercise sessions: resistance exercise that loads the bones is most effective
Eat and drink enough
NASA found 6 to 7 sessions a week effective to keep bone in spaceflight

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Medical Technical Brief 013: Bone Loss, pp. 2-3, 12-14, 16, 19

name: Immune system
measureInSpace: Baseera measures nothing here: this system is coloured by the symptoms you log. NASA asks crews about allergies, rashes, infections and wound healing, and monitors immune function.
whyCheck: NASA says the immune system can be affected by the stress of long-term life in microgravity, and by poor nutrition.
hazardEffects: Stress, long stays in microgravity and too little food can weaken immune function. NASA lists infections such as throat infections and influenza among conditions seen in flight.

whenToAct.crew: Act when you log a fever, rash or other infection symptom: tell the flight surgeon. A rash that does not fade under a glass needs emergency help.
whenToAct.surgeon: NASA keeps countermeasures in place to sustain immune measures within the normal range, and uses a pre-flight health stabilization programme.

prevention: Sleep, eat and drink enough
Report infection symptoms early

name: Eyes
function: Let you see and judge distance.
measureInSpace: Baseera measures nothing here: this system is coloured by the symptoms you log. NASA schedules eye exams during long missions.
whyCheck: Some astronauts develop vision changes on long missions. About 16% show swelling of the optic disc during or after long missions, most of it mild.
hazardEffects: NASA believes the eye changes (called SANS) are linked to fluid shifting towards the head in microgravity, and possibly to diet or the environment.

whenToAct.crew: Act when your vision changes in any way: tell the flight surgeon.
whenToAct.surgeon: NASA monitors for SANS and can provide glasses with stronger lenses. Countermeasures are still being researched.

prevention: Report vision changes early
Keep your scheduled eye exams
